newsitem.title: UK: No change election boosts dlr at least short term.
newsitem.headline: No change election boosts dlr at least short term.

text.p: The American electorate's decision to maintain the governmental status quo was met with some relief on foreign exchange markets, and after rising gently overnight dollar/yen at least looked well underpinned in Europe.

Although a second presidential term by Bill Clinton had been discounted, the market was concerned about the fate of the Houses of Congress although the Republicans appeared to heading for control of both.
"More of the same is the best of both worlds," said Nick Parsons, currency strategist at Banque Paribas in Paris.
"It's the best mix for the bonds so by default it's the best mix for the dollar," Parsons added.
Dollar/yen continued its overnight climb in Europe and by 0714 GMT it had got to 114.65/75 compared with around 113.80 when the early results pointed to another win for Bill Clinton.

Dollar/mark was a little more restrained and ran into some light profit-taking in initial European dealings, to stand at 1.5233/40 marks after a peak of 1.5261 and 1.5140 as the early results came in.
But with the big event out of the way it remains to be seen whether the dollar can continue firm, some doubt it can.
The question mark that hangs over the dollar now stems from the fact that ahead of the election the U.S. had a clear interest in a firm dollar policy in order to keep asset markets underpinned.

With Wall Street is still in the stratosphere and the bond market very firm it can be argued that both are overdue for a shakeout. If there is to be a fall in asset markets, best get it out of the way early in the administration, analysts said.
"The last thing (Treasury Secretary Robert) Rubin wanted was a dollar fall which would have reflected a lack of international confidence in the Clinton administraton," Parsons said.
Against the background of a presidency that could be more relaxed about both asset markets and the dollar, the global consensus for a firm dollar may start to break down.

For the first time in around a decade industrialised nations have had a vested interest in a firmer dollar. But dollar/yen is near levels where Japan no longer needs a continued yen depreciaton and dollar/mark is at levels where Germany might start to get jittery about the inflationary impact.
"The big risk is a policy change," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International. "But a policy change would be initiated only by the U.S., not the Japanese or the Germans."

U.S. auto-makers have recently sought to address the problem of the firmer dollar with the government, and if the Democrats had won the House of Representatives there would have been greater pressure for a change of dollar policy, analysts said.

But at the end of the day a lot depends on what happens to the domestic economy. "If the U.S. economy slows down and the auto-makers start to hit difficulty they will start to demand a softer dollar," DKB's Lyons said.
Significantly, both Honda and Toyota are, or are thinking of, shifting production from the U.S. back to Japan indicating the weakness of the yen has had a big impact on costs in Japan.

"If that became more widespread it could affect sentiment," Lyons said. "The risk of a policy shift in the States and the fact that firms are maybe moving production back to Japan could stabilise dollar/yen for the moment."

The short-term dollar's performance very much depends on the U.S. bond market reaction, and at present it looks like it will take the result well. But given recent firmness it may well yet turn into a case of "buy the mystery, sell the history.'
"Bonds firmed yesterday on the belief that the Republicans would hold the House of Representatives, and they have," Parsons said. "You have to ask where the fresh buying will come from."
